q: Small fine scissors with straight or curved blades narrowing to blunt tips.
u: Divides/dissects extraocular muscles and tendons, especially during recession and resection for strabismus.

q: Broad, stout scissors with uniformly curved blades and blunt tips.
u: Cuts the optic nerve with its sheaths during enucleation.
note: Enucleation Scissors & Enucleation Guide (Wells Enucleation Spoon) — Enucleation Scissors: Stout, strong, curved scissors with blunt tips. Enucleation Guide / Spoon: Curved metallic spoon with a central U-shaped slot/notch to engage the optic nerve. Procedure (Enucleation): Surgical removal of the entire eyeball (globe) after peritomy, detaching all 6 extraocular muscles, sliding the enucleation guide behind the globe to engage the optic nerve, and severing the optic nerve with the stout curved enucleation scissors. Indications for Enucleation: 1. Intraocular Malignant Tumors: Retinoblastoma (in children; requires cutting a long stump of the optic nerve, 10-15 mm) and Malignant Melanoma of the Choroid (in adults). (Evisceration is contraindicated in tumors). 2. Painful Blind Eye: E.g., Absolute Glaucoma, Neovascular Glaucoma. 3. Severe Perforating / Crushing Ocular Trauma: Badly mutilated globe with no visual potential (done to prevent Sympathetic Ophthalmitis in the fellow eye). 4. Phthisis Bulbi or Non-bleeding Anterior Staphyloma (for cosmetic fitting of an ocular prosthesis). Viva Distinction - Atrophic Bulbi vs. Phthisis Bulbi: Atrophic Bulbi: Shrunken, non-functional eye where internal tissue organization is still preserved; has a quadrilateral (square) shape due to the pull of the four rectus muscles on the hypotonic globe. Phthisis Bulbi: End-stage shrunken, completely disorganized, fibrosed, and calcified eyeball with severe hypotony.

q: Metallic ball with a pointed tip on a handle; brass retains heat longer than steel.
u: Heated and applied to bleeding points for hemostasis; the PDF also lists bare sclera, corneal ulcer margin and small iris prolapse.
note: Ball-Point Thermal Cautery — Design: Metallic handle with a round copper/brass ball and a pointed tip. Use: Heated over a spirit lamp and applied to the bare sclera after peritomy to cauterize bleeding episcleral vessels (hemostasis) before making the scleral incision in cataract or glaucoma surgery. This added note is in addition to the existing thermocautery (heat cautery) card text — keep both.

q: Bent-tip 26-gauge needle fitted to a 2 mL syringe.
u: Makes anterior capsulotomy; the syringe can maintain the anterior chamber with BSS or Ringer’s lactate during manipulation.

q: Angular fine hook attached to a long, round, solid handle.
u: Dials/centres the IOL and positions haptics; may also rotate, crack or chop the nucleus and break posterior synechiae.
note: IOL Dialler (Sinskey's Hook) — Identification: It is an angular fine hook attached to a long round solid handle. Methods and Uses: a) It is used to dial the IOL for the purpose of centration and bringing the IOL haptics into horizontal position. The hook is positioned in the dialing holes of the optic of IOL and then rotated in clockwise manner. b) It may be used as a left-hand instrument during phacoemulsification: To rotate the lens nucleus. To crack the lens nucleus after doing quadrant trenching. To chop the nucleus. Video note — Sinskey Hook (IOL Dialer): Design: Slender handle with an angled shaft ending in a tiny, blunt, right-angled hook (no teeth). Uses: 1. Dialing and positioning the IOL into the capsular bag or ciliary sulcus. 2. Nucleus manipulation in SICS (prolapsing the nucleus into the anterior chamber). 3. Used as a second instrument through the side-port in Phacoemulsification to rotate and divide/chop the nucleus.

q: Shown as “No hole dialer” in the PDF figure.
u: The PDF labels the image but gives no separate identification details or use.

q: Shown as “chopper” in the PDF figure.
u: The PDF labels the image but gives no separate identification details or use.

q: Round or oval wire ring at the end of a narrow limb; may be slightly spoon-shaped.
u: Used to remove a subluxated/dislocated lens or deliver the nucleus in ECCE with an irrigating vectis.
note: Vectis (Wire Vectis) — Identification: It is a ring of wire (round or oval) at the end of a narrow limb, attached to a handle (like a large platinum loop). It may be a little curved like a spoon. Method: Pupil must be fully dilated. Never pass it blindly. The lens edge should be visible. Carefully pass the vectis behind the lens. Lift the lens and then take the lens out. Vitreous loss is inevitable in vectis delivery. Sometimes, a sector iridectomy is needed instead of peripheral iridectomy. Open-sky vitrectomy is done after lens delivery. Lens-Loop / Vectis — Uses: a) To remove a subluxated or dislocated lens. b) To deliver the nucleus in ECCE with irrigating vectis. If the vectis is not available, these instruments may be used as vectis: a) End of McNamara's spoon. b) Intracapsular forceps. Here, apply forceps with closed tips, carefully pass them behind and then open the tips a little so that the lens sits on them. Now, lift the lens and remove it. Video note — Wire Vectis: Design: Oval wire loop attached to a handle (plain or irrigating). Use: Used in SICS and ECCE to deliver the lens nucleus out of the anterior chamber (by sliding the loop beneath the nucleus and extracting it while depressing the posterior scleral lip). Also used to extract a dislocated/subluxated lens.

q: Hollow vectis with a needle base and 3–5 small openings at the tip.
u: Irrigation creates hydrostatic pressure while the vectis mechanically delivers the nucleus.

q: Elongated S- or Z-shaped instrument with two long, narrow, flattened, blunt ends.
u: Repositions iris after lens/nucleus delivery or iridectomy; can also break synechiae.

q: Two-way cannula: one end connects to irrigation tubing; the cannula connects to a syringe for aspiration.
u: Simultaneous irrigation and aspiration of cortical material after ECCE; can remove viscoelastic or blood.
note: Two Way Irrigation & Aspiration Cannula — It is available in various designs, commonly used are Simcoe's classical or reverse cannula. Uses: a) For irrigation and aspiration of the lens matter in ECCE. b) Aspiration of hyphaema. Video note — Simcoe Irrigation and Aspiration (I/A) Cannula: Design: Two-way cannula with a curved/direct tip. One port is connected to an IV infusion line (for continuous irrigation), and the other port is attached to a 10 mL or 5 mL syringe via silicon tubing (for manual aspiration). Use: Used through the side-port or main tunnel for cortical wash (aspiration of lens cortex) and viscoelastic/hyphema wash. Video note — Simcoe I/A Cannula: Available as Direct, Indirect/Reverse, and J-shaped Simcoe cannulas for manual cortical cleanup.

q: Long straight instrument with a flat spoon/spatula at each end.
u: Used with the lens expressor for pressure-counterpressure lens delivery in the Smith-Indian technique.

q: Flat corrugated handle with a curved, olive-pointed blunt tip; the tip plane is perpendicular to the handle’s flat plane.
u: Applies pressure at the lower limbus and supports the lower pole of the lens; also used for nucleus delivery.

q: Solid handle with a long narrow limb bent 90° at the tip; tip may be sharp or knobbed.
u: Hooks extraocular muscles during squint, retinal-detachment and enucleation operations.

q: Long, narrow, solid cylindrical instrument with a smooth conical pointed tip and corrugated body.
u: Dilates the punctum/canaliculus before lacrimal cannula insertion or probing.
note: Punctum Dilator (Nettleship's) — Identification: It is a long narrow solid cylindrical instrument with a smooth conical pointed tip. Its body is corrugated for better gripping with thumb and index finger. Method of Syringing: a) Anaesthetize the eye with 4% lignocaine or 1% proparacaine drop. b) Pull the lower lid and identify the lower punctum in bright light. c) Hold the punctum dilator vertically by right index and thumb and place it on the punctal opening. d) Twist it with light pressure and introduce into the punctum. e) Then hold the punctum dilator horizontally and push it medially by rotatory movement following the course of the canaliculus (first vertically then horizontally). Then withdraw it. f) Take the lacrimal cannula, fitted in a syringe, filled with distilled water and introduce it in the same direction. g) Push the piston of the syringe to inject water into the canaliculus and ask the patient whether water has reached the throat or not. Alternatively note the swallowing movement of the neck. Uses: a) To dilate the punctum and part of the canaliculus before introducing lacrimal cannula for syringing. b) To dilate the punctum for probing in case of congenital dacryocystitis. c) To dilate the punctum and then probing to identify lacrimal sac during DCR operation. d) For dilatation of the punctum in congenital or acquired punctal stenosis. e) Before Dacryocystography (DCG). f) May be used as a marker (by dipping the pointed tip in gentian violet) in squint or retinal detachment operation. Video note — Nettleship's Punctum Dilator: Design: Corrugated metal handle with a fine, conical pointed tip. Use: Used to dilate the lacrimal punctum before diagnostic syringing or probing.

q: Thin long probe with a rounded tip; different sizes (00–08), with two sizes on a flat handle.
u: Probes the nasolacrimal passage and helps identify the lacrimal sac position during DCR.
note: Lacrimal Probes (Bowman's) — Identification: These are a set of straight metal wires of varying thickness (0-8) with blunt rounded ends and flattened central platform. Uses: a) To probe nasolacrimal duct in congenital block. b) To identify the lacrimal sac during DCT and DCR operations. Video note — Bowman's Lacrimal Probe: Design: Thin, malleable wire probes of graduated thicknesses. Use: Used for therapeutic probing of the nasolacrimal duct in Congenital Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (CNLDO) (if conservative Crigler massage fails after 6-12 months of age) and diagnostic probing in canalicular block.

q: Long narrow instrument with a stout pointed dissector at one end and an elongated scoop at the other.
u: Bluntly dissects the lacrimal sac; the scoop removes tissue remnants in DCT.

q: Spring handle with two blades: upper blade has a sharp-edged hole; lower blade has a cup-like depression.
u: Punches lacrimal/nasal bone to create the bony ostium in DCR.
note: Added-note label: The existing card is Kerrison bone punch; this added note is the user's Bone Punch transcription — keep both, do not replace the existing card. Bone Punch — Identification: Consists of a stout spring handle and two blades attached at right angle. The upper blade has a small hole with a sharp cutting edge. The lower blade has a cup-like depression. Uses: To enlarge the bony opening during DCR operation by punching the bone from margins of the opening. (Carelessness during this step can cause accidental damage to the nasal mucosa and the nasal septum.)

q: Saddle-shaped folded blade at the end of a handle; not self-retaining.
u: Retracts the upper lid for anterior-segment examination, especially in children or patients with blepharospasm/photophobia.

q: Small fork-like instrument with downward-bent ends.
u: Retracts skin, subcutaneous tissue and ligament during lacrimal sac surgery.

q: Large shallow rectangular or oval spoon attached to a handle; spade-like.
u: Scoops intraocular contents during evisceration while the sclera is left intact.
note: Evisceration Scoop — Identification: Consists of a small but stout rectangular blade with slightly convex surface and blunt edge attached to a handle. Use: To separate out the uveal tissue from the sclera during evisceration operation. Video note — Evisceration Spoon / Scoop: Design: Shallow, oval/rectangular metallic scoop on a handle. Procedure (Evisceration): After excising the cornea, the evisceration scoop is used to scoop out all the inner contents of the globe (lens, vitreous, retina, and uveal tract), leaving the outer scleral shell and extraocular muscles intact. (Note: All uveal pigment must be thoroughly scraped off the sclera to prevent Sympathetic Ophthalmitis). Indications for Evisceration: 1. Panophthalmitis: Severe purulent inflammation of the entire globe including Tenon's capsule. (Note: Enucleation is strictly contraindicated in Panophthalmitis because cutting the optic nerve opens the subarachnoid meningeal sheaths, allowing infection to spread to the brain causing meningitis or cavernous sinus thrombosis. In panophthalmitis, a frill excision of the sclera is done, leaving a small collar of sclera around the optic nerve for drainage). 2. Expulsive Choroidal Hemorrhage: Rare, catastrophic intraoperative bleeding from choroidal vessels (due to sudden hypotony or uncontrolled hypertension). 3. Bleeding Anterior Staphyloma: Ectatic, protruding cornea lined by uveal tissue that is actively bleeding.

q: Flat solid plate about 10 cm long, with rounded convex ends.
u: Provides support under the lid during lid surgery such as ptosis and entropion repair; does not provide hemostasis.

q: Stout two-limbed clamp with a screw, semilunar plate and corresponding U-shaped rim; right/left versions.
u: Fixes the lid and helps hemostasis during entropion surgery; reduces the operative field.
note: Lid Clamp or Entropion Clamp — Identification: Consists of a D-shaped plate opposed by a U-shaped rim, which when tightened upper and left lower lid and the second for right lower and left upper lid. While applying the lid clamp, the plate is kept towards the conjunctival side, the rim on the skin side, and the bandwheel with the help of a screw, clamps the tissues. Two clamps are required: one can be used for right is always situated on the temporal side. Advantage over lid spatula: It is a self-retaining instrument and does not need an assistant to hold. Disadvantages: a) Operative field is less. b) Pressure necrosis can occur if fitted tightly. Uses: Used in lid surgery, e.g. entropion, ectropion corrections - protects the eyeball, supports the lid tissue and provides haemostasis during surgery. NOTE: part of this description in the user's photograph is blurred/cut off — do not invent the missing wording; preserve this limitation in the card. Video note — Snellen's Entropion Clamp: Design: Has a flat, D-shaped metal plate (inserted into the conjunctival fornix beneath the lid to protect the globe) and a fenestrated U-shaped rim that clamps over the skin surface via a screw. Uses: Used in Entropion surgery (and other lid surgeries) to immobilize the eyelid and provide hemostasis (bloodless surgical field).

q: Serrated squeeze-action handle; makes a clean 0.75 mm round hole without tissue tags.
u: Creates a full-thickness opening/trap door after the scleral flap in trabeculectomy.
note: Kelly's Descemet's Membrane Punch (Trabeculectomy Punch) — Design: Squeeze-action guillotine punch with a small cutting head at the tip. Use: Used in Trabeculectomy (glaucoma surgery for open/closed-angle glaucoma) to punch out a block of deep corneoscleral tissue (containing the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal) beneath a partial-thickness superficial scleral flap. This creates a guarded fistula allowing aqueous humor to drain from the anterior chamber into the subconjunctival space (forming a filtering bleb).

q: Two parallel arms (probe and guide) connected to the shaft; right- and left-sided versions.
u: The internal arm is threaded into Schlemm’s canal using the external parallel arm as a guide.

q: Marker with a patterned marking head.
u: Guides optimal placement of sutures in keratoplasty.

q: Cylindrical instrument with circular blade, adjustable inner core/obturator and protective cover.
u: Cuts donor and recipient corneal buttons in penetrating and lamellar keratoplasty.
note: Corneal Trephine (Castroviejo's) — Identification: It is a cylindrical instrument which has three parts: a) A circular blade. b) An adjustable inner core or 'obturator'. c) A cover to protect the sharpness of the blade. It is available in different diameters (like 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 7.5, 10, 10.5, etc. in mm). The obturator has a scale (marking 0.2, 4.6, etc. in 1/10th of mm) which helps the surgeon to select exact depth of the cornea to be cut. This is important in lamellar keratoplasty. Uses: To cut the donor and recipient corneal button in penetrating and lamellar keratoplasty.

q: Spring-adjusted measuring calliper with pointed ends and a scale in millimetres.
u: Measures corneal size and surgical dimensions such as incision length, scleral flap, muscle recession/resection and corneal button size.
note: Caliper (Castroviejo's) — Identification: It is a measuring calliper in which the measurement (in mm) is adjusted by spring action of screw. Ends are pointed like a compass, and scale is fixed to the opposite end. Methods: The exact measurement is taken by adjusting the spring action of the screw, which is indicated by the pointed end on the scale. Uses: To measure the size of the cornea, as in buphthalmos, megalocornea, microcornea, etc. To use in various surgeries: a) Phacoemulsification or SICS - length of incision. b) Trabeculectomy - length of scleral flap. c) Squint operation - amount of resection or recession of muscle. d) Keratoplasty - to determine the size of the donor and recipient corneal button. e) Retinal detachment surgery to measure the distance for passing encircling band. f) IOFB removal - to measure the site of incision for IOFB removal. g) Ptosis surgery - to measure the amount of LPS to be resected. h) To measure length for any purpose. Video note — Castroviejo Callipers: Design: Dividers with pointed tips, a graduated millimeter scale (0-20 mm), and an adjusting thumbscrew. Uses: 1. Cataract Surgery: Measuring the length of the scleral incision in SICS. 2. Pars Plana Intravitreal Injections & Vitrectomy Ports: Measuring the exact distance behind the limbus to safely enter the pars plana without damaging the lens or retina: 4.0 mm behind the limbus in Phakic eyes. 3.5 mm behind the limbus in Pseudophakic eyes. 3.0 mm behind the limbus in Aphakic eyes. 3. Corneal Diameter Measurement: Measuring white-to-white corneal diameter (e.g., in Congenital Glaucoma / Buphthalmos, Microcornea, Megalocornea, or for ACIOL sizing). 4. Strabismus (Squint) Surgery: Measuring the amount of extraocular muscle recession or resection. 5. Ptosis Surgery: Measuring the amount of LPS (Levator Palpebrae Superioris) muscle resection.

q: Medium-sized spring needle holder with two narrow, fine, curved jaws.
u: Holds fine needles (6-0, 8-0 and 10-0) for corneoscleral, scleral, corneal and mucosal-flap suturing.
note: Needle Holder (Barraquer's) — Identification: It is a medium-sized spring needle holder with two narrow and fine curved jaws. It may be available with or without a catch. Uses: It is used to catch fine needles (5-0, 6-0, 8-0 and 10-0 sutures) for: a) Corneoscleral suturing after cataract operation. b) Scleral suturing in squint, detachment and trabeculectomy operations. c) Corneal suturing in penetrating injury or keratoplasty. d) Suturing the mucosal flaps in DCR operation. e) Sometimes in conjunctival suturing. Video note — Barraquer Microsurgical Needle Holder: Design: Fine, curved jaws with spring-action handles (available with or without a lock; the one demonstrated has no lock to prevent tissue jerking when releasing the needle). Use: Used for corneoscleral, corneal, and conjunctival suturing (e.g., with 10-0 Nylon or 8-0 Vicryl).

q: Sponge-holding instrument shown under this heading.
u: The PDF supplies the heading and photograph, but no separate description or use.

q: Towel clamp shown in the page-38 photograph.
u: The PDF supplies the heading and photograph, but no separate description or use.

q: Spoon-shaped instrument shown under this heading.
u: After the recti muscles are severed, it is passed deep into the orbit from the lateral side to hold the optic nerve before it is cut.
note: Optic Nerve Guard (Wells Enucleation Spoon) — Identification: It is a spoon-shaped instrument with a central cleavage. Uses: To engage the optic nerve during enucleation. Video note — Enucleation Scissors & Enucleation Guide (Wells Enucleation Spoon): Enucleation Scissors: Stout, strong, curved scissors with blunt tips. Enucleation Guide / Spoon: Curved metallic spoon with a central U-shaped slot/notch to engage the optic nerve. Procedure (Enucleation): Surgical removal of the entire eyeball (globe) after peritomy, detaching all 6 extraocular muscles, sliding the enucleation guide behind the globe to engage the optic nerve, and severing the optic nerve with the stout curved enucleation scissors. Indications for Enucleation: 1. Intraocular Malignant Tumors: Retinoblastoma (in children; requires cutting a long stump of the optic nerve, 10-15 mm) and Malignant Melanoma of the Choroid (in adults). (Evisceration is contraindicated in tumors). 2. Painful Blind Eye: E.g., Absolute Glaucoma, Neovascular Glaucoma. 3. Severe Perforating / Crushing Ocular Trauma: Badly mutilated globe with no visual potential (done to prevent Sympathetic Ophthalmitis in the fellow eye). 4. Phthisis Bulbi or Non-bleeding Anterior Staphyloma (for cosmetic fitting of an ocular prosthesis). Viva Distinction - Atrophic Bulbi vs. Phthisis Bulbi: Atrophic Bulbi: Shrunken, non-functional eye where internal tissue organization is still preserved; has a quadrilateral (square) shape due to the pull of the four rectus muscles on the hypotonic globe. Phthisis Bulbi: End-stage shrunken, completely disorganized, fibrosed, and calcified eyeball with severe hypotony.
